title: Landscape-Dependent Performance of Photonic Quantum Solvers in QUBO Feature Selection for Financial Risk Detection
abstract: Feature selection for imbalanced classification tasks such as credit card fraud and consumer default detection requires balancing predictive relevance, inter-feature redundancy, and computational feasibility. We benchmark three computing paradigms, classical branch-and-bound optimization (Gurobi), photonic entropy computing (QCI Dirac-3), and simulated photonic boson sampling (Piquasso), across thirteen feature-selection methods on two datasets: ULB Credit Card Fraud (30 features) and AmEx consumer default (159 features). Each method is routed to the solver matched to its mathematical structure. On ULB, Dirac-3 MI-Spearman matches the all-features model using 13 of 30 features (mean F1 0.873 +/- 0.023 over five runs, best run 0.896), and Piquasso is the best method at k=5. On AmEx, performance rises steadily with the feature budget and every paradigm approaches F1 = 0.80 only near the full feature set. Most differences between Gurobi and Dirac-3 on identical methods fall within run-to-run variation; the large gaps occur where the certified optimum generalizes poorly, most sharply for distance correlation on AmEx at k=25 (Gurobi F1 = 0.422 vs. a Dirac-3 mean of 0.746). At matched budgets, F1 varies about ten times more across methods on ULB than on AmEx, which we trace to how concentrated the predictive signal is in each feature space.
summary: This paper compares classical and photonic quantum solvers for feature selection in financial risk detection using two large datasets. It demonstrates that the choice of solver and method is critical, showing that quantum approaches can outperform classical methods when the underlying feature signal is highly concentrated. This highlights the potential role of quantum computation in solving complex, structured optimization problems in finance.
main_problem: The paper addresses feature selection for imbalanced financial classification tasks by comparing classical optimization methods against photonic quantum solvers.
main_result: Photonic solvers (Dirac-3) showed superior performance over classical solvers (Gurobi) in certain scenarios, particularly when the predictive signal is highly concentrated in a small feature subset (ULB dataset).
method: The authors benchmarked three computing paradigms—classical branch-and-bound, photonic entropic computing, and photonic boson sampling—across various QUBO and graph-theoretic feature selection methods.
model_or_system: The model involves formulating feature selection as a combinatorial optimization problem, utilizing two financial datasets: ULB Credit Card Fraud and AmEx Consumer Default. The computational platforms include classical solvers and photonic quantum devices.
key_observables: F1 score (primary metric), Gini Coefficient, and Jaccard similarity, used to quantify classification performance and feature redundancy.
important_parameters: Feature budget ($k$), dataset size (30 vs. 159 features), and the specific mathematical structure of the objective function (QUBO, higher-order terms).
main_assumptions: The comparison assumes that the mathematical structure of the feature selection method dictates the appropriate quantum or classical solver, and that the performance gap between solvers is measurable.
figures_summary: The notes reference tables and matrices showing F1 and Gini scores across various methods and feature budgets for both datasets, and similarity matrices illustrating feature overlap.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem (feature selection for imbalanced data), details the datasets and the three computational paradigms (Gurobi, Dirac-3, Piquasso), systematically compares performance across multiple methods (Tier 1, 2, 3), and analyzes the dependence of performance on dataset structure and feature budget.
why_interesting: The work directly tests the practical utility of quantum computation (photonic solvers) for solving complex, real-world optimization problems arising in data science, providing empirical benchmarks for quantum advantage in optimization.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Solver-aware method routing: each tier is assigned to the solver that handles its mathematical structure exactly (solid arrows). Tier 1 and Tier 2 QUBO methods are also run on Dirac-3 for a direct, method-matched comparison (dashed arrows).

Figure 2: F1 versus feature budget k for the best solver and method in each tier, together with Piquasso. For each tier, the line shows the solver–method pair with the highest F1 at any budget (Table 4; ties broken by the smaller k, then by the higher mean F1 across budgets), plotted at every budget. Dirac-3 values are five-run means with 95% CI error bars; Gurobi values are deterministic and Piquasso values were identical across repeated runs. The dotted line is the all-features model. †AmEx Tier 3 uses the 135-feature pre- filtered pool, so its largest budget is k=130.

Figure 3: Mean off-diagonal Jaccard similarity among QUBO/Graph feature-selection methods as a func- tion of relative feature budget k/n, for ULB and AmEx. Error bars show 95% CI across five independent Dirac-3 runs (Tables 15 and 16). The dashed line is the expected similarity between two random subsets of the same size (Eq. 9). Both datasets lie on this curve at every tested budget, so cross-method overlap does not separate them.
